title: How Evolution in Isolation Works
summary: Hosts discuss how animals evolve in isolation, starting from the theory of evolution and common ancestry. They cover speciation, using black bears and polar bears as the example of parapatric speciation, and reproductive isolation as the point where speciation is complete. They then turn to evolutionary bottlenecks, including a genetic defect in a small Amish community in Pennsylvania, and to iguanas displaced by Hurricane Marilyn that floated from Guadeloupe to Anguilla, presented as a natural experiment testing the island rule. The episode opens with a sponsor line for the 2012 Camry and closes with a pointer to HowStuffWorks.

segments.title: Opening sponsor read and greeting
segments.summary: A Camry sponsor line opens the episode, followed by the hosts' greeting and introduction of the topic.

segments.title: Speciation and reproductive isolation
segments.summary: The hosts define speciation as one species becoming two or more. They explain parapatric speciation using black bears and polar bears, then say speciation is complete only after reproductive isolation.

segments.title: Evolutionary bottlenecks and the Amish
segments.summary: The hosts describe an evolutionary bottleneck as a small group cut off from the main population, which can spread genetic defects. They cite a group of Amish in Pennsylvania with smaller-than-normal brains (microcephaly), a trait that proved fatal.

segments.title: Iguanas displaced by Hurricane Marilyn
segments.summary: The hosts describe iguanas that Hurricane Marilyn carried from Guadeloupe to Anguilla, where there had been none before. They present it as a natural experiment for testing bottlenecks and the island rule on whether island iguanas grow larger or smaller. The episode closes with a sign-off pointing to HowStuffWorks.
